Begin by defining the authorized product set and collecting genuine reference units through the brand owner or a licensed distributor. Photograph each unit under consistent lighting and record dimensions, weight, materials, serial-number format, package construction, security labels, and expected manufacturing tolerances. Store those records in a controlled evidence system with purchase receipts and chain-of-custody notes. Do not acquire suspected fakes from an illicit seller merely to create a collection; use customs seizures, donated samples, or a vendor-approved test set.

A first-line reviewer can check print alignment, color consistency, stitching or molding quality, spelling, barcodes, and the relationship between the package and the item. Treat one mismatch as a lead rather than proof, because legitimate products can have redesigns and regional variants.

For online monitoring, search public listings using lawful brand terms, image similarity, price anomalies, repeated seller language, and duplicated photographs. Preserve the listing URL, timestamp, seller identifier, screenshots, product claims, and payment or contact details that are publicly visible. Do not impersonate buyers, make test purchases outside policy, or attempt to access a seller’s account. Route high-confidence cases to counsel, the platform’s reporting channel, customs, or law enforcement.

For physical distribution, train receiving staff to quarantine suspicious stock, avoid reselling it, and document the handoff. Use serialized inventory, approved suppliers, purchase-order matching, and periodic audits. A useful workshop can compare a genuine item with a clearly marked training replica and ask trainees to explain which observations require laboratory confirmation.

This approach teaches materials analysis, packaging review, marketplace monitoring, evidence preservation, and escalation while protecting consumers and respecting trademark law. It addresses the underlying operational problem—how counterfeit supply chains are recognized and stopped—without enabling their manufacture or sale.

The physical product usually looks close to an authentic item but differs in material feel, dimensions, weight, print registration, stitching or molding, adhesive, serial format, security label, barcode, or package construction. Reviewers should compare a suspected unit with an authenticated reference under controlled lighting and record observations, photographs, supplier claims, batch information, and chain of custody. A single difference is a lead, not proof, because genuine products change across regions and production years.

The online listing often reuses official photographs, descriptions, logos, and product language. Preserve the public URL, seller identifier, timestamp, screenshots, claims, and publicly visible contact details before the listing changes.

The fulfillment pattern can reveal a larger network. Stock may appear at multiple small storage points, storefronts may share payment or contact indicators, and orders may originate from different shipping locations. Investigators should connect listings through image hashes, wording, account behavior, inventory anomalies, and public logistics information rather than relying only on a shop name. Do not impersonate buyers, access accounts, or make unauthorized purchases.

At intake, quarantine suspicious stock and photograph it as received. A second reviewer verifies serials against a restricted registry and checks whether the claimed batch and supplier exist. Laboratory analysis may be needed for inks, polymers, metals, or electronics. Escalate high-confidence findings to counsel, the marketplace, customs, or law enforcement.

Preventive controls include approved suppliers, purchase-order matching, serialized inventory, segregation of duties, periodic audits, watermarking, image matching, and an authorized-channel lookup. The profile teaches recognition, evidence preservation, and disruption without giving instructions for reproducing marks, sourcing blanks, pricing fakes, or hiding their distribution.
